name: Chocolate
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, restlessness, excessive urination, tremors, seizures, elevated heart rate
action: Emergency vet immediately. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are most dangerous; milk chocolate is still toxic in quantity.
lethal_dose_note: Toxic threshold approximately 20mg theobromine/kg. Baking chocolate ~390mg/oz; milk chocolate ~44–64mg/oz.

name: Xylitol (Sugar-Free Products)
symptoms: Vomiting, weakness, lethargy, ataxia (incoordination), seizures, liver failure
action: Emergency vet immediately. Xylitol triggers insulin release causing hypoglycemia and can cause acute liver failure.
lethal_dose_note: As little as 0.1g/kg can cause hypoglycemia; 0.5g/kg associated with liver failure.

name: Grapes & Raisins
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, abdominal pain, decreased urine output, kidney failure
action: Emergency vet immediately. No safe dose known — even one grape can cause kidney failure in some dogs.
lethal_dose_note: Toxic dose unknown; idiosyncratic — some dogs tolerate it, others do not. Do not take the risk.

name: Onions & Garlic
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, pale gums, elevated heart rate — symptoms may be delayed 3–5 days
action: Contact vet. Allium toxicity destroys red blood cells causing hemolytic anemia. Cooked, powdered, and dehydrated forms are just as dangerous.
lethal_dose_note: >0.5% body weight (any allium). Garlic is ~5× more toxic than onion per weight.

name: Macadamia Nuts
symptoms: Weakness, hyperthermia, vomiting, tremors, lethargy (within 12 hours of ingestion)
action: Contact vet today. Usually not fatal but can cause significant distress and may need supportive care.
lethal_dose_note: As few as 2.4g/kg can cause clinical signs.

name: Avocado
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, fluid accumulation. Pit is a choking hazard and contains high concentration of persin.
action: Contact vet. The flesh is mildly toxic due to persin; the pit is a dangerous obstruction risk.
lethal_dose_note: Persin: toxic dose not well-established in dogs, but the pit ingestion is the primary emergency concern.

name: Alcohol
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, incoordination, central nervous system depression, difficulty breathing, coma
action: Emergency vet immediately. Dogs are much more sensitive to ethanol than humans.
lethal_dose_note: Even small amounts can be fatal depending on body weight.

name: Caffeine (Coffee, Tea, Energy Drinks)
symptoms: Restlessness, rapid breathing, elevated heart rate, tremors, seizures
action: Contact vet immediately. Caffeine and methylxanthines are toxic to dogs.
lethal_dose_note: Toxic dose around 140mg/kg; coffee grounds and tea bags are highly concentrated.

name: Raw Yeast Dough
symptoms: Bloating, abdominal distension, vomiting, disorientation (ethanol produced by fermentation)
action: Emergency vet. Yeast dough expands in the stomach and produces ethanol — double danger.
lethal_dose_note: Stomach can rupture from expansion. Treat as emergency.

name: Nutmeg
symptoms: Tremors, seizures, disorientation, hallucinations, elevated heart rate
action: Contact vet immediately. Myristicin is the toxic compound. Small amounts cause GI upset; larger doses are neurologically dangerous.
lethal_dose_note: Toxic above ~1 teaspoon for a medium dog.

name: Apple Seeds & Fruit Pits
symptoms: If significant amounts ingested: vomiting, breathing difficulty (cyanide poisoning)
action: Contact vet if a large number of seeds or pits were consumed. Small amounts are unlikely to cause harm — the concern is the amygdalin (cyanide precursor) inside.
lethal_dose_note: Flesh is safe; seeds and pits contain amygdalin. Large quantities are the concern.

name: Chives
symptoms: Same as onion/garlic — hemolytic anemia, vomiting, weakness
action: Contact vet. Part of the allium family — equally toxic to onions and garlic.
lethal_dose_note: Toxic at >0.5% body weight.

name: Leeks
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, hemolytic anemia, pale gums
action: Contact vet. Allium family — same mechanism as onion.
lethal_dose_note: Any quantity warrants a vet call.

name: Mushrooms (Wild)
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, liver/kidney failure (Amanita species), neurological signs
action: Emergency vet. If you cannot positively ID a mushroom as safe, treat as potentially deadly (Amanita phalloides is fatal with no antidote).
lethal_dose_note: Amanita phalloides: a single cap can be fatal. Never guess with wild mushrooms.

name: Rhubarb
symptoms: Drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, kidney failure (with large amounts)
action: Contact vet. The leaves are most toxic; stalks less so but still problematic.
lethal_dose_note: Leaves contain soluble oxalates and anthraquinones.

name: Cherries
symptoms: GI upset; seeds/pits contain cyanide-releasing amygdalin
action: Remove pits before giving any cherry. Pitted cherry flesh in very small amounts is not acutely toxic, but pits, stems, and leaves contain amygdalin. Avoid to be safe.
lethal_dose_note: Pits are the hazard; a few pitted cherries are unlikely to cause harm.

name: Tomatoes (Green/Unripe)
symptoms: Weakness, cardiac effects, GI upset (solanine toxicity)
action: Ripe red tomatoes in small amounts are generally safe; the green parts (leaves, stems, unripe fruit) contain solanine and should be avoided.
lethal_dose_note: Ripe tomatoes: low risk. Green parts: moderate concern.

name: Dairy Products
symptoms: Diarrhea, gas, vomiting (lactose intolerance)
action: Many dogs are lactose intolerant. Small amounts of hard cheese or plain yogurt are often tolerated; large amounts of milk, ice cream, or soft cheese can cause GI upset.
lethal_dose_note: Not toxic; digestive intolerance.

name: Raw Salmon & Trout
symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, fever, lethargy (Salmon Poisoning Disease — Pacific Northwest specific)
action: In Pacific Northwest regions, raw salmon can carry Neorickettsia helminthoeca which can be fatal. Cook salmon fully. Other raw fish carry parasites but salmon poisoning is the most serious concern.
lethal_dose_note: Salmon Poisoning Disease can be fatal if untreated; very treatable with antibiotics if caught early.

name: Cooked Chicken (Plain)
symptoms: None
action: Plain cooked chicken (no seasoning, no onion, no garlic) is safe and easily digestible. Good as a bland diet addition.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Cooked Turkey (Plain)
symptoms: None
action: Plain cooked turkey without seasonings, skin, or bones is safe.
lethal_dose_note: Safe. Avoid skin (high fat) and avoid with stuffing (onion/garlic).

name: Carrots
symptoms: None
action: Excellent low-calorie snack. Both raw and cooked are safe. Good for teeth. High in beta-carotene.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Blueberries
symptoms: None
action: Safe in moderation. High in antioxidants. Excellent treat option.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Watermelon (Seedless)
symptoms: None
action: Hydrating and safe. Remove seeds and rind. The rind can cause GI upset.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Peanut Butter (Xylitol-Free)
symptoms: None (if xylitol-free)
action: Safe and popular treat. ALWAYS check the label — some brands use xylitol which is deadly. Choose natural, unsalted varieties. High in fat, so moderate amounts.
lethal_dose_note: Safe if xylitol-free. Always check the label.

name: Peanuts
symptoms: None in small amounts
action: Unsalted, plain peanuts are safe in small amounts. High fat content — too many can cause digestive upset or pancreatitis.
lethal_dose_note: Safe in moderation. Avoid salted varieties.

name: Bananas
symptoms: None in moderation
action: Safe in small amounts. High in sugar so limit for diabetic or overweight dogs.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Apple (Flesh Only)
symptoms: None (flesh only)
action: Remove core and seeds. The flesh is safe and a good source of fiber and vitamin C.
lethal_dose_note: Safe (flesh only). Seeds contain amygdalin — remove them.

name: Cooked Eggs
symptoms: None
action: Fully cooked eggs are a good protein source. Raw eggs carry Salmonella risk and contain avidin which inhibits biotin absorption — cook them.
lethal_dose_note: Cooked: safe. Raw: not recommended.

name: Cooked White Rice
symptoms: None
action: Safe and easily digestible. Classic bland diet staple alongside boiled chicken for GI upset.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Cooked Sweet Potato
symptoms: None
action: Excellent source of vitamins. Serve plain and cooked (no butter, no seasoning). Remove skin for easier digestion.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Cucumber
symptoms: None
action: Low calorie, hydrating snack. Safe and well-tolerated.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Pumpkin (Plain)
symptoms: None
action: Plain pumpkin puree (not pie filling) is excellent for digestive health. High in fiber, helps with both diarrhea and constipation.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Green Beans
symptoms: None
action: Safe and nutritious. Good low-calorie treat or food extender for overweight dogs.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Broccoli
symptoms: GI upset in large amounts; isothiocyanates can irritate the digestive tract
action: Safe in very small amounts (less than 10% of daily diet) as occasional treat. Larger amounts cause significant GI upset.
lethal_dose_note: Florets are lower risk; stalks are a choking hazard.

name: Corn (Off the Cob)
symptoms: None (kernels only)
action: Corn kernels are safe in moderation. The cob is a choking and obstruction hazard — never give a dog the whole cob.
lethal_dose_note: Kernels: safe. Cob: obstruction emergency risk.

name: Mango (Pitted)
symptoms: None in moderation
action: Remove skin and pit. The flesh is safe and nutritious. Pit is a choking hazard and contains cyanide.
lethal_dose_note: Safe (flesh only).

name: Peaches (Pitted)
symptoms: GI upset if too much; pit contains cyanide (amygdalin)
action: Remove the pit and stem entirely. The flesh in small amounts is safe; the pit is toxic and a choking hazard.
lethal_dose_note: Flesh: safe in small amounts. Pit: toxic.

name: Strawberries
symptoms: None in moderation
action: Safe and a good source of vitamin C. High in sugar; limit for overweight or diabetic dogs.
lethal_dose_note: Safe.

name: Cooked Salmon (Fully Cooked)
symptoms: None
action: Excellent source of omega-3 fatty acids. Must be fully cooked — raw salmon can carry Salmon Poisoning Disease (fatal if untreated).
lethal_dose_note: Cooked: safe and beneficial. Raw: serious risk.

name: Spinach
symptoms: In very large amounts: kidney stress from oxalic acid
action: Safe in very small quantities. Not recommended as a regular food due to oxalic acid content which can affect kidney function. Not a concern in tiny amounts.
lethal_dose_note: Small amounts: negligible risk. Avoid in dogs with kidney disease.

name: Coconut & Coconut Oil
symptoms: Loose stools, diarrhea if too much fat
action: Not toxic, but high in medium-chain triglycerides. Small amounts are generally fine. Too much can cause GI upset. Coconut water is high in potassium — avoid.
lethal_dose_note: Not toxic; digestive tolerance varies.

name: Milk
symptoms: Diarrhea, gas, vomiting (lactose intolerance)
action: Most adult dogs are lactose intolerant. Small sips are unlikely to harm, but avoid regular feeding. Puppies can digest mother's milk; cow's milk is still problematic.
lethal_dose_note: Not toxic; lactose intolerance issue.

name: Honey
symptoms: Blood sugar spike in diabetic dogs; botulism risk for puppies
action: Safe for healthy adult dogs in very small amounts. Do not give to diabetic dogs or puppies under 1 year (botulism risk from Clostridium spores).
lethal_dose_note: Not toxic for healthy adults; contraindicated for puppies and diabetic dogs.

name: Cinnamon
symptoms: Irritation to mouth, skin, or digestive tract; if inhaled: coughing, choking
action: Not acutely toxic, but irritating in large amounts. Small amounts in food are generally fine. Cinnamon oil is concentrated and more of a concern.
lethal_dose_note: Not toxic in small amounts. Large amounts of cinnamon oil can cause problems.

name: Raw Meat (General)
symptoms: Salmonella, Listeria, Campylobacter infection; parasites
action: Raw meat carries bacterial and parasitic risks to both pets and people in the household. If feeding raw, use commercially prepared, pathogen-tested raw food. Avoid raw pork (trichinosis risk).
lethal_dose_note: Risk varies by source and handling. Not inherently toxic but carries pathogen risk.

name: Mushrooms (Store-Bought, Common)
symptoms: None for standard edible varieties
action: Common grocery store mushrooms (button, portobello, shiitake) are safe for dogs when plain and cooked. Wild mushrooms are a different story — never assume wild mushrooms are safe.
lethal_dose_note: Store-bought edible varieties: safe. Wild: potentially deadly.

name: Bread (Plain)
symptoms: None (small amounts)
action: Plain bread in small amounts is not toxic. No nutritional benefit and high in carbohydrates. Avoid bread with raisins, onion, garlic, or xylitol.
lethal_dose_note: Safe (plain). Bread with raisins/garlic/xylitol is dangerous.

name: Popcorn (Plain, Air-Popped)
symptoms: Choking on unpopped kernels; GI upset from buttered or salted varieties
action: Plain, air-popped popcorn in small amounts is safe. Avoid buttered, salted, or flavored popcorn. Watch for unpopped kernels which are choking hazards.
lethal_dose_note: Plain is safe. Flavored varieties can be problematic.

name: Peas
symptoms: None in moderation
action: Fresh or frozen peas are safe. Avoid canned peas (high sodium). Some concern about peas in grain-free diets and dilated cardiomyopathy — discuss with your vet if it's a primary ingredient.
lethal_dose_note: Safe as occasional treat.
